title: Physical properties of matter
competency: Describe physical properties and use them to identify substances.

keywords.def: A property we can measure or observe without changing what the substance is.
A property that depends on the amount of sample: length, mass, volume.
A property that does not depend on the amount: density, colour, melting point, hardness.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid. Ice: 0 °C.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. Water at sea level: 100 °C.
Mass per unit volume: d = m/V, in kg/m³.
The ability of a substance to conduct electricity.

en.text: A physical property can be measured or observed without changing what the substance is. Colour, odour, taste, state, melting point, boiling point, density and conductivity are physical properties. Melting ice is still water, so melting point is a physical property.

screens.title: Still water?
screens.ask: You measure the temperature at which ice melts. Is the water still water afterwards?
opts: No, it becomes a new substance
screens.after: It is still water. Measuring the melting point did not change what it is. That is a physical property.

screens.title: 2.2.1 Physical properties of matter
paras: Substances are identified by their properties.
A physical property can be measured and observed without changing the composition.
Melting ice gives water. Water differs from ice only in appearance.
We can freeze the water to get ice back.
So melting point is a physical property.

screens.title: Physical properties detected by sense organs
table: Chalk is white, water is colourless, gold is yellow
Water is odourless, flowers are fragrant, orange is fruity
Honey is sweet, lemon is sour, table salt is salty
screens.note: Caution! Smell and taste only safe substances. Never taste anything in the laboratory.

screens.title: Physical state
paras: Physical state is the form of a substance at a given temperature and pressure.
Water is solid below 0 °C, liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C, and gas above 100 °C.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A property we can measure or observe without changing what the substance is.

screens.why: Looking at colour does not change the copper.
screens.clue: Which one leaves the substance the same?

screens.why: We see colour, smell odour and taste with the tongue.

screens.ask: Honey is sweet, table salt is salty and lemon is ___.

screens.text: You may taste lemon at home but never an acid in the laboratory. Why?
opts: Laboratory acids may be strong and harmful
screens.ans: Laboratory acids may be strong and harmful
screens.why: Tasting is only used when the substance is not harmful. Lab acids can burn or poison.

screens.text: At what temperatures is water a liquid (at sea level)?
screens.why: Below 0 °C water freezes; above 100 °C it is a gas. In between it is a liquid.
screens.clue: Use the melting point and the boiling point.

en.text: Extensive properties depend on how much sample you have: length, mass, volume. Intensive properties do not: density, colour, melting point, hardness. Intensive properties help us tell substances apart, because they do not change from sample to sample.

screens.title: Cup or bucket
screens.ask: A cup of water and a bucket of water. Which is the same for both?
screens.after: Both boil at 100 °C. Mass and volume depend on how much water there is.

screens.title: Two kinds of physical property
paras: Extensive physical properties depend on the amount of sample. Examples: length, diameter, mass, volume.
Intensive physical properties do not depend on the amount. Examples: density, colour, melting point, hardness.
Intensive properties help us tell substances apart.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A property that depends on the amount of sample: length, mass, volume.
A property that does not depend on the amount: density, colour, melting point, hardness.

screens.why: A small or big piece of ice melts at 0 °C.
screens.clue: Does it change if you have more?

screens.why: Extensive: changes with the amount. Intensive: stays the same.
screens.clue: Imagine twice as much. Does it change?

screens.text: Dawit has two gold rings: a small one and a big one. Which property helps prove both are gold?
screens.why: Density is intensive: pure gold has the same density in any amount. Mass and volume differ between the rings.
screens.clue: Choose a property that does not depend on size.

en.text: Some physical properties are measured with apparatus. They have constant values under set conditions. Melting point is when a solid melts: ice at 0 °C. Boiling point: water boils at 100 °C at sea level. Density is mass per volume, d = m/V. Electrical conductivity is how well a substance carries electricity; metals conduct well.

screens.title: Measure it
screens.ask: Which tool do you need to find the melting point of ice?
screens.after: Melting point is a temperature, so we measure it with a thermometer.

screens.caption: A thermometer measures melting and boiling points.

screens.title: Measurable physical properties
paras: These can be measured with apparatus.
They have constant values under specific conditions.
table: Temperature at which a solid becomes liquid
Temperature at which a liquid boils
Water boils at 100 °C at sea level

items: Needs a balance and a cylinder.
screens.why: Colour, odour and taste are sensed. The others are measured.

screens.ask: A stone has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 cm³. Its density is ___ g/cm³.
screens.clue: Divide the mass by the volume.

screens.ask: A block of wood has a density of 0.5 g/cm³ and a volume of 40 cm³. Its mass is ___ g.
screens.clue: Turn d = m/V around: m = d × V.

items.text: Which of these physical properties have constant values under specific conditions?
items.why: Measurable properties have constant values under set conditions.

items.text: Which can be recognized directly by our sense organs?
items.why: We smell odour, see colour and taste with the tongue.

items.text: What will happen to ice kept in a cup in the classroom?
items.why: The room is warmer than 0 °C, the melting point of ice.

items.text: How do you describe the taste of lemon?
Why are you never allowed to taste any acid in the laboratory?
opts: Laboratory acids may be strong, harmful or contaminated
items.ans: Laboratory acids may be strong, harmful or contaminated
items.why: Tasting is used only when a substance is not harmful.

test.why: Measuring it does not change the substance.

test.ask: Water boils at ___ °C at sea level.
test.why: The boiling point of water at sea level is 100 °C.
Mass depends on the amount of sample.

test.text: The interaction of a substance with light results in its …
test.why: Colour results from the interaction with light.
